paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Dearborn County, Indiana, took place in late May 1903, after the murder of Rosa Kaiser near Manchester Station was blamed on Black men and a Black suspect, Louis Everson, was threatened with lynching at Lawrenceburg. Everson was released and stoned out of town by a mob, and farmers then ordered Black families and workers out of the county, about 100 by one estimate. The murder remained unsolved in September.

Rosa Kaiser and her father, Martin Kaiser, were attacked while walking home from church; he was clubbed and thrown into a creek, and she was killed. Her body was found on 23 May in West Fork, a branch of Tanner's creek near Guilford. That afternoon Coroner Sales returned a verdict of murder by persons unknown, "believed to have been two negroes" seen nearby, and a post-mortem found she had not been sexually assaulted. The Big Four Railway was then rebuilding its line through the area with gangs that included many Black laborers.

Everson, known as "Black Ponto," was arrested at Cleves, Ohio, and brought to the Lawrenceburg jail on 23 May for his protection; he denied any part in the crime. As farmers poured into town that night, Sheriff Axby barricaded the jail and placed a heavy guard. On 24 May farmers gathered at Lawrenceburg, Guilford and Manchester and "openly threatened lynching"; the Associated Press wrote that Everson would have been lynched had a witness identified him.

On the evening of 25 May Sheriff Axby and two officers walked Everson down the Big Four tracks past the city limits and told him to leave. A "hooting mob of men and boys" followed him for a mile, cursing, stoning and beating him, until he escaped into woodland. He was arrested again at Dillsboro the next morning, released at once, and "left on the run."

Meanwhile Louis Kaiser, a brother of the dead girl, circulated a petition asking the Big Four contractors to dispense with "colored labor," and the Indianapolis Journal warned of a "war of extermination" if they refused. A wire report said every Black person within five miles of Manchester had been ordered to leave. By 28 May an Indianapolis dispatch estimated that 100 Black people had been driven out of the county's rural districts in three days, as families were ordered out and farm hands discharged. A committee headed by Martin J. Kaiser Jr. told the Big Four superintendent at Guilford that his Black workers must go; he said he would conform, though work would stop because white men could not be had.

Within days the girl's father and her uncle, Frank Aust, said the killer was probably a white man, and a reported assault on two girls at Weisburg, first blamed on a Black worker, was traced to a white infirmary inmate. No arrest of anyone who stoned Everson or drove out Black residents appears in the coverage. In September the sheriff arrested Otto Pholenz, alias Pool, a Big Four worker, at Cincinnati as a suspect; he denied any knowledge of the crime.

The Indianapolis Journal's Lawrenceburg correspondent gave the fullest account, first headlining the girl as "Victim of an Unknown Negro's Crime" and then, three days later, "May Have Been White Man." Elsewhere the story came by wire: the Seattle Star headlined "Human Brute Is Still at Liberty" and said lynching or burning "cannot be avoided" if guilt were established, and the AP's account of the threats ran from South Dakota to Wisconsin.

The expulsion drew pointed headlines: the Washington Times printed it as "Indianians Solving the Negro Question," and the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic in Arkansas as "Another 'Southern Outrage' Perpetrated in Indiana." The Plymouth Tribune in Indiana called it a "Crusade Against the Colored Man Because One Was Suspected of a Brutal Crime." The only Black-press item found, in the Savannah Tribune on 30 May, reprinted the wire under "Making War on Negroes" without comment.

Reports put the attack on Wednesday, Thursday or Friday night, and the later wire names the girl Anna rather than Rosa. The Seattle Star said the father blamed "a colored man," but later Lawrenceburg reports said he never saw his assailant.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Dearborn County, Indiana
bases: After a white girl's murder was blamed on Black men, crowds threatened to lynch a jailed Black suspect, a mob stoned and beat him as officers sent him out of town, and farmers ordered Black families and workers out of Dearborn County, about 100 by one estimate (A8, A9, A12, A13).

The lynching threats are reported by separate Indianapolis Journal and Courier-Journal specials and the AP (A3, A4, A8); the stoning by an Indianapolis Journal special (A9); the expulsion by two different wire stories and the Journal's report of the petition (A9, A12, A13).

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal first called the girl a 'victim of an unknown negro's crime' and wrote of 'her negro slayer', then three days later ran 'May Have Been White Man.'
The Seattle Star headlined 'Human Brute Is Still at Liberty' and wrote that lynching or burning 'cannot be avoided' if guilt were established.

The Washington Times ran the expulsion as 'Indianians Solving the Negro Question'; the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic as 'Another "Southern Outrage" Perpetrated in Indiana', turning it against Northern critics of the South.
The Plymouth Tribune (Ind.) printed the wire as 'Driving the Negroes Away: Crusade Against the Colored Man Because One Was Suspected of a Brutal Crime.'
The Savannah Tribune printed the wire as 'Making War on Negroes. Farmers in Dearborn County, Indiana, Avenging a Murder,' with no editorial comment.
